The views of Latin American governments toward Cuba are surveyed in a CIA paper dated January 1, 1961. The American break with Havana was days away, and the region was picking sides fast. Mexico stood apart from the rest, as it often did on Cuba.

Most other governments leaned toward Washington, though with varied warmth. The paper sets out each stance as analysts read it at the new year. For readers, it is a map of the hemisphere at a turning point. The lines drawn that winter would hold, with few changes, through the invasion spring that followed.

Many voices, not one, must shape arms deals, argues Resolution A/69/54, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its theme is the push for joint, many-sided work in disarmament and against the spread of arms. The text recalls a 2001 vote that tied such work to the fight against terror, and a chain of votes since 2002 on the same theme.

The UN's core aim frames the call: to guard peace by joint steps that head off threats and halt attacks on the peace. Arms questions, in this view, are too big for any one state or bloc to settle alone. Deals struck by all, the Assembly holds, are the deals that last.

Palestine crossed a legal line in Security Council Resolution 54, passed on 15 July 1948. The stopgap state of Israel had agreed in the main to stretch the truce in the land. The states of the Arab League had turned down plea after plea, from the UN mediator and from the Council, to do the same. Fighting had flared up anew in the land as a result.

The Council rules that the state of Palestine is a threat to the peace, in the terms of Article 39 of the Charter. It orders all states and chiefs in the fight to halt all armed acts. Cease-fire orders must go out to their troops, at a time the mediator will fix. It was the first such ruling of the young Council's life.

Mathijs Baens, Heidi Noels, Vicky Broeckx, and co-authors exposed a flaw in a beloved lab tool in a 2006 paper. EGFP, a glowing green protein from jellyfish, is attached to other proteins so scientists can watch them move inside living cells. Labs worldwide trusted it as a passive tag that changes nothing.

The team found the dark side of that title: EGFP shows defective polyubiquitination, meaning the cell's tagging system for disposing of proteins handles it abnormally. A marker that bends the very process under study can mislead experiments on protein breakdown, a field central to cancer and brain disease. Security Council Resolution 754, adopted on May 18, 1992, recommended Slovenia for membership in the United Nations. The Alpine republic had broken from Yugoslavia in June 1991 and held its freedom through a short war.

The Assembly seated Slovenia on May 22. Admission mattered beyond form: Yugoslavia's seat was in dispute, and each successor republic needed its own place in the world body. The short resolution is one step in the legal unmaking of a federation, taken while wars in Croatia and Bosnia were still raging.

Flash-WAM distills a large multimodal world model into a smaller one, with modality-aware distillation that respects what each sense contributes. The goal is compact world models cheap enough to run inside real robots and agents.
arxiv-2606-05554: Economists assume people dislike risk, but does risk aversion actually change anything when risks shift over time? This irrelevance theorem shows that under time-varying risk, risk aversion can wash out — preferences that look important prove mathematically irrelevant. The result trims a beloved assumption down to where it truly matters.
arxiv-2606-05654: Content moderators judge posts written in code-mixed language — Hindi-English, Spanglish — but the same content in different surface forms gets different verdicts. This paired study shows surface form changes moderation decisions, exposing workflow instability. Inconsistent moderation is unfair moderation, and the paper quantifies exactly how shaky it is.
arxiv-2606-05754: Fiber optic cables can hear — distributed acoustic sensing turns them into thousands of microphones. This paper advances Sagnac-assisted enhanced phi-OTDR for that task, with a standardized benchmark and engineering evaluation framework. Standard tests let the industry compare sensing systems honestly instead of cherry-picking results.
arxiv-2606-06054: Personal AI agents remember your life — but retrieving memories by similarity alone surfaces plausible-sounding falsehoods. This paper moves beyond similarity to trustworthy memory search: retrieval that weighs evidence and provenance. Trustworthy memory is what separates a helpful assistant from a confident fabulist.
arxiv-2606-06154: Personalizing a foundation model on each user's device — federated adaptation — is expensive when done naively. This paper amortizes the cost with hypernetwork-driven LoRA: one network that generates personalized adapters cheaply. Amortized personalization makes private on-device AI practical for everyone.
arxiv-2606-06254: Pruning a code model to run cheaper risks dulling its defenses — especially against adversarial code mutations that sneak past. SecRL-Prune uses structured reinforcement learning to prune CodeLLMs while preserving that adversarial robustness. The method keeps models lean without making them gullible.
arxiv-2606-06554: Terahertz spectroscopy fingerprints polymers — but the spectra are subtle. This multi-scale feature attention network classifies polymers from those fingerprints, attending across scales. The method turns faint THz wiggles into reliable material IDs. Non-destructive testing gets a powerful new eye.
arxiv-2606-06754: Grading analytic essays usually needs trained models or tired humans. MADRAG scores them training-free: multi-agent debate with retrieval-augmented generation, where agents argue about the essay's merits. Debate plus evidence makes for fairer automated grading. The method grades essays without any training.
arxiv-2606-07254: Tracking non-Abelian quantum states over long horizons needs falsifiers — tests that catch wrong models. This held-out transition-pair falsifier does that job. The falsifier keeps long-horizon tracking honest. Wrong quantum models must be caught early. Principled falsification keeps long-horizon tracking honest.
tob-10554:
James Legge rendered Lao Tzu's eighty-one chapters again here under the fuller title The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and Its Characteristics. Legge, the Scottish missionary who became Oxford's first professor of Chinese, translated with a scholar's precision and copious notes. His version first made Chinese philosophy legible to many English readers.

The paradoxes remain intact, starting with the warning that the Tao that can be named is not the eternal Tao. Chapters on ruling without interference, the strength of weakness, and the uses of emptiness follow. Readers meet a Victorian landmark of translation, where careful notes surround verses that resist every attempt to pin them down.
tob-13554:
Extracts from al-Ghazali's Ihya, his Revival of the Religious Sciences, present some religious and moral teachings in digestible portions. Intention, gratitude, patience, and the diseases of the heart are among the subjects drawn from that vast manual. Al-Ghazali wrote the Ihya after his spiritual crisis, to rebuild religious life from the inside.

Shorter and more directly useful than his autobiography, these selections show the theologian as moral physician, diagnosing pride, envy, and heedlessness and prescribing remedies. The Ihya became Islam's classic manual of the inner life. Readers pressed for time can meet its central teaching here, then turn to the Confessions for the author's own story.
tob-4054:
Volume one of a four-volume edition of H. P. Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine carries the subtitle Cosmogenesis, Theosophy's creation story in full. Blavatsky presents stanzas from a claimed archaic book, the Book of Dzyan, surrounded by her vast commentary. The universe unfolds through cycles, rounds, and planes across unimaginable spans of time.

Hindu time-cycles blend with Victorian geology and evolutionary language as spirit descends toward matter. The commentary argues with contemporary science while borrowing its scale. Readers beginning the four-volume set should expect density and digression; the opening volume lays the cosmology on which the later volumes build their accounts of humanity, symbolism, and hidden history.
tob-4254:
A French study of Haitian Vodou spirits appeared in 1918 under the title Les Daimons du Culte Voudo, credited to the pen name Her-Ra-Ma-el. European readers of its day knew Vodou mostly through rumor and fright. The study instead catalogs the lwa, the spirits of the cult, one by one.

Rites, offerings, songs, and the families of spirits receive orderly treatment. Rada and Petro nations, healing and work spirits, the dead and the waters: the pantheon takes shape for a French audience. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book stands as an early European attempt to describe Haitian religion as its worshippers practice it.
afr-200-2-ufo-reporting-1954:
The Air Force gave its UFO hunt a rule book on August 12, 1954. Regulation 200-2 names the things UFOBs, sets the reporting chain for the whole service, and clamps the press line on hard cases. Chief of Staff Nathan Twining signed the order himself.

Each sighting of weight was to move up the chain in set form, with care and speed. Only a small desk in Washington could speak in public on the cases that stayed unsolved. The rule was Blue Book's spine for its whole life. It turned saucer reports into office routine across the whole force.
ennemoser-history-of-magic-vol-1-1854:
Joseph Ennemoser gave magic a grave past in The History of Magic, Vol. I, in English dress from 1854. William Howitt turned the German text to English. Ennemoser was a healer who held that trance and dreams hint at deep laws of the mind. He traces rites from old tribes to the age of the church.

Dreams, spells, and wild cures get a fair, calm look. He treats the theme as fit for true study. The pair of tomes is the age's great past of magic. This first half lays the broad base. Howitt, who turned the text, was a poet and tale smith too. His smooth prose helped the dense German work find a wide English crowd.
ennemoser-history-of-magic-vol-2-1854:
Joseph Ennemoser brings his long past of magic to a close in The History of Magic, Vol. II, in English from 1854. William Howitt's turn of the German text fills this tome as in the first. The tale runs on through witch hunts, seers, and the trance cures of Ennemoser's own day and land.

He asks what part is fraud, what part is law of mind. His calm, grave tone sets the work past mere tales of spooks. Read with the first tome, it is the age's chief past of magic. Its reach spans two fat tomes. Ennemoser came from the Tyrol hills and healed the sick by trance. His own cures feed the last parts of this long, grave survey.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen works through the kings in Vol. 2 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1854. The first tome laid out sources and script. Here the tale runs king by king, age by age, as Bunsen fits Egypt's long line into the frame of the world's past as his age knew it.

Lists, dates, and clashes with the Good Book fill the tome. His sums are now seen as too grand in span. Yet his reach taught the field to think big. The work is a vast, brave try.
brewster-more-worlds-one-1854:
David Brewster was a Scots man of science famed for his work on light. His More Worlds than One came out in 1854. The book is a direct reply to Whewell's tract of the year past. Its full title calls it the creed of the thinker and the hope of the Christian.

Brewster holds that a wise God would not leave vast worlds bare of life. He works through the planets and stars with the best facts of the day. Faith and star science walk side by side in his case. The book kept the claim of many lived-in worlds in fine health.
theologia-germanica-1854:
Theologia Germanica is a small book of soul lore from 1300s Germany. No name sits on the work; a priest of Frankfurt may have wrote it. Susanna Winkworth gave it English dress in 1854. Martin Luther had praised the book three hundred years past.

The text bids the soul let go of self will and rest in God. It sets the life of Christ as the path each soul must walk. Calm, plain words hide a deep and hard call to yield all. The wee book swayed Luther, the first church rebels, and mystics since.
thoreau-walden-1854:
Henry David Thoreau published Walden in 1854, his experiment in deliberate living at Walden Pond. The book is the founding text of environmental thought and simple-living philosophy in the American tradition today. Thoreau lived two years in a cabin he built on Emerson's land by the pond.

He tills beans, watches ants war, and sounds the pond's depth through winter ice in Concord. Economy preaches cutting wants, while Brute Neighbors and Winter Animals crowd the pages with keen natural seeing in detail. The seasons turn one full round, spring's thaw standing for the soul's rebirth in his famous close here. Simplify, simplify is the book's household motto, and its challenge still nettles comfortable readers in every age. Few American books have been reread so often for so many different reasons.
nerval-daughters-of-fire-1854:
Gérard de Nerval published Daughters of Fire in 1854, his linked stories, here in English translation for readers. The set holds Sylvie, Émilie, and Octavie, the dreamlike heart of French Romanticism in its late flower. Nerval, who walked a lobster on a blue ribbon in Paris, wrote these tales between spells of madness.

Sylvie, the crown of the set, shuttles between a village girl, a dancer, and a lost actress in Valois. Memory and present blur until the narrator cannot tell which love, or which year, he truly inhabits at all. Octavie and Émilie mix travel, theatre, and occult longing in Nerval's limpid, haunted prose of dream and waking. He hanged himself in 1855, weeks after the book appeared, and France slowly learned what it had lost in him. Proust and the surrealists later claimed these tales as scripture.
philo-yonge-vol1-1854:
Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher of the first century who read the Torah through Greek philosophy. Yonge's 1854 first volume of his complete works in English appeared in Bohn's Classical Library. It made Philo's full range open to Victorian readers for the first time.

Philo treats the stories of Genesis as allegories of the soul while holding fast to Jewish law and worship. His idea of the Logos, the divine word that orders the world, bridges Greek thought and later Christian theology. This volume holds his accounts of creation and the lives of the patriarchs.
edwards-freedom-of-will-1754:
Edwards's Inquiry into the Freedom of the Will, published in 1754, is the American Calvinist's great work of philosophy. He wrote it against Arminian writers who taught that the will must be free from all motive to be moral. The book defends determinism joined to moral agency.

Edwards argues that the will always chooses as the strongest motive inclines it, and that this costs us no true liberty. A person is free, in his account, when nothing stops him from doing what he most wants. The argument's tight logic still anchors debate on freedom, sin, and responsibility.
philo-yonge-vol2-1854:
Volume two of Yonge's Works of Philo Judaeus, published in 1854, holds Philo's allegorical commentaries on Genesis. Here Philo reads the creation story and the lives of the patriarchs as maps of the soul. The great treatises on the creation and on the virtues stand in this volume.

Abraham's journey becomes the soul's schooling, Sarah and Hagar become wisdom and its handmaid, and each command hides an inner sense. Yonge's plain Victorian English keeps Philo's dense Greek argument readable for students without the language. The volume shows Philo's fusion of Torah and Platonism at its most inventive.
philo-yonge-vol3-1854:
Volume three of Yonge's Philo, published in 1854, gathers the historical and apologetic works. Philo steps out of allegory here to defend his people before Rome and record their recent past. The Life of Moses and the Embassy to Gaius anchor the volume.

The Embassy tells how Philo led a Jewish delegation to the emperor Caligula after riots against the Jews of Alexandria. His account is an eyewitness record of Jewish life under Roman power at a moment of crisis. Historians prize this volume beside the allegories, since it preserves facts found in few other sources.
philo-yonge-vol4-1854:
Volume four of Yonge's Philo, published in 1854, completes the first English Philo with the Questions and Answers on Genesis and Exodus. Philo poses a question on a verse, then answers it on two levels, the literal and the allegorical. The form shows his classroom method at work.

Why did God plant a tree in Eden, why did Cain build a city, and what do the plagues of Egypt mean? Each answer turns law and story into teaching on the soul's growth and God's care. With this volume, English readers gained the whole surviving Philo in their own tongue.
feuerbach-essence-christianity-eliot-185:
Ludwig Feuerbach's Essence of Christianity appeared in English in 1854, translated by Marian Evans, who wrote as George Eliot. Feuerbach, a German philosopher, argued that God is a picture of human nature itself. The translation was Eliot's only work published under her real name.

Feuerbach held that qualities praised in God, such as love, wisdom, and justice, are human qualities projected upward. Religion, then, is humanity worshipping its own best image without knowing it. The argument shook German and British thought and fed later critiques of religion. Eliot's clear English carried the work into Victorian debates about faith, doubt, and what worship really means.
nott-gliddon-types-mankind-1854:
Josiah Clark Nott and George Robins Gliddon published Types of Mankind in 1854 in Philadelphia. Nott was an Alabama physician and Gliddon a popular lecturer on Egypt. Their large, illustrated treatise argued for polygenism, the claim that human races were created separately and unequally.

Chapters on skulls, ancient monuments, and natural history built a case that served the defense of slavery in America. The book was a bestseller and a scientific scandal at once, praised by slaveholders and attacked by clergy and later scientists. Modern scholars cite it as a foundational text in the history of scientific racism. It is kept and studied as evidence of how science was bent to serve bondage.
racine-phedre-french-1854:
Jean Racine wrote Phèdre in 1677, at the height of his career as France's leading playwright. The text here is the French original, in the Didot edition of 1854. Phèdre, wife of King Theseus, burns with a forbidden love for her stepson Hippolytus and cannot master it.

Phèdre's confession sets off a chain of lies, rage, and deaths. Theseus curses his son, Hippolytus dies, and Phèdre takes poison after clearing his name. Racine tells the tragedy in strict, shining verse, with few characters and great pressure. French readers rank Phèdre as the summit of their classical theater, a study of passion and shame.
keller-green-henry-1854:
Gottfried Keller, the Swiss writer, published Green Henry in German in 1854 and 1855. The text here comes from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, since no English translation is in the public domain. Heinrich Lee, nicknamed for his green coat, tells the story of his own youth and failed hopes.

Heinrich dreams of painting, drifts to Munich, and learns how thin his talent runs. Love, money trouble, and pride delay his return to his patient mother in Zurich. Keller drew the tale from his own life, softened by humor and hindsight. The novel ranks beside Wilhelm Meister among German artist novels. Its rich village and city scenes made it the great Swiss novel of growth.
bentivoglio-wars-of-flanders-1654:
Guido Bentivoglio, a cardinal who had served as papal nuncio at Brussels, wrote Della guerra di Fiandra in 1632. Henry Carey's English translation of 1654 gives it as The Compleat History of the Warrs of Flanders. The war in question is the Dutch Revolt, the Eighty Years' War of the Netherlands against Spain.

Bentivoglio watched that war from the Spanish side of the lines, with a diplomat's access to councils and commanders. His history tells the Counter-Reformation case with grace, fairness, and rare inside knowledge. He praises brave foes and blames folly on his own side. The work stands as the great Catholic history of the revolt, and a model of the historian's craft.
boole-laws-of-thought-1854:
Seven years after his first pamphlet, George Boole issued An Investigation of the Laws of Thought in 1854. The longer book gives the mathematical theories of logic and of probabilities. Boole widens his calculus from classes to whole statements that can be true or false. Reasoning and chance both come under his symbols.

He works out how to test arguments and how to weigh uncertain evidence. The system lets a reader compute with thought itself, in a strict sense. Later logicians refined his tools, but the leap was his. The book made logic a branch of mathematics. Its effects reached far past philosophy. Modern computing descends from it.
dods-spirit-manifestations-1854:
Dods answered the spirit rapping craze in Spirit Manifestations Examined and Explained, from 1854. Judge Edmonds, a noted believer, had defended the rappings as true spirit speech. Dods, the electrical psychologist, refuses that reading outright. The wonders, he argues, flow from minds and bodies under electrical laws.

He examines famous cases and mediums with his rival system in hand. The book records the passage from mesmerism to spiritualism in America. It speaks from the mesmerist side of that divide. Dods had built his name before the Fox sisters' knocks were heard. His defense of an older wonder against a newer one fascinates. Historians prize the primary view it gives.
zoist-vol-12-1854:
April 1854 to January 1855 fills the twelfth volume of The Zoist. Elliotson's long campaign for mesmerism nears its end in print. Reports still come in: cures under trance, operations without pain, and clairvoyant cases. Cerebral physiology holds its place beside the mesmeric record.

Britain is at war in the Crimea as these pages appear. The journal's world of provincial practice goes on regardless. Thirteen volumes, from 1843 to 1856, would complete the set. Volume twelve is the last full year but one. Its value lies in the unbroken chain of cases. Together the volumes let readers judge the movement from inside.
borlase-antiquities-cornwall-1754:
Cornwall's oldest stones drew William Borlase to write a county history unlike most others of its time. His Antiquities, Historical and Monumental, of the County of Cornwall came out in 1754. Borlase, a clergyman and keen observer of nature, spent years visiting sites across the far west of England.

Stone circles, cromlechs, and carved stones fill his pages, each one noted, drawn, and placed in its setting. Borlase linked many of these remains to the Druids, as writers of his age often did. Later students of old monuments still start with his record, since some sites have since changed or vanished.
king-american-eclectic-dispensatory-1854:
John King compiled The American Eclectic Dispensatory in 1854, a huge guide to the plant remedies of his school. King taught in Cincinnati, a center of eclectic medicine, which chose the best cures from every system. His book tells doctors what each drug is, how to prepare it, and when to use it.

Roots, barks, and herbs fill the entries, many of them native American plants little known in Europe. King gives doses, cautions, and the forms a medicine might take, from teas to extracts. For historians, the volume is the dispensatory of American botanical practice, a full shelf of plant lore in one binding.
pratt-voice-of-warning-1854:
Parley P. Pratt wrote A Voice of Warning in 1837, and the eighth edition of 1854 shows how long it kept selling. Pratt, an apostle and tireless missionary of the young Mormon church, aimed his tract at every reader he could reach. Prophecy, the Book of Mormon, and the coming kingdom of God fill its urgent pages.

No Mormon tract of the nineteenth century was reprinted more often or carried farther. Missionaries bore it across America and Britain, and converts often met the faith first in Pratt's clear voice. The book's warnings of judgment and calls to gather shaped how outsiders pictured the new movement for decades.
murchison-siluria-1854:
Roderick Murchison, a British geologist, named the Silurian system after an ancient Welsh tribe. His Siluria, published in 1854, sums up years of fieldwork in Wales and beyond. It is the founding text for one great slice of earth's past.

Murchison maps the old rock layers and the fossils that mark them. He traces the same system through England, Europe, and America. The work fixed the order of the oldest fossil-bearing rocks and gave geology a firm time scale. Later disputes over its borders only showed how central the book was. Welsh hills and quarries supply many of his best proofs.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-geography-v:
William Smith edited his Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography in the 1850s, with Volume One, from Abacaenum to Hytanis, in 1854. It is the great Victorian gazetteer of the ancient world. Smith's scholars worked from the classical authors and from travelers' reports.

Each place gets its history, its coins, its ruins, and the ancient authorities that name it. Cities, rivers, mountains, and islands of Greece and Rome fill the pages. Woodcuts of sites and plans help the reader picture lost towns. Classical students used it to map every campaign and voyage in their texts. A companion set on ancient life and customs shares the same editor and plan.

Volume Two of Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography, also 1854, completes the gazetteer, from Iabadius to Zytus. A general index closes the set. William Smith's team matched the biography dictionary in scale and care.

The entries trace the rest of the ancient map: Italy's towns, the provinces, and the edges of the known world. Histories of sieges, colonies, and trade routes gather under each name. Coins and remains ground the literary record in things a reader could still see. The two volumes together gave Victorian readers the fullest ancient atlas in words that English has produced.
plos-pone-0003454:
Bahareh Vali and co-authors studied liver damage in people with two viruses in this 2008 paper. Hepatitis C harms the liver faster when HIV is also present. The immune reasons for that speed-up were unclear. The team looked for HIV-specific T cells inside the liver.

They examined patients co-infected with hepatitis C and HIV-1. T cells aimed at HIV were indeed found gathered in liver tissue. Fighters meant for one virus may add harm in the other's organ. That misplaced buildup could help explain the faster liver disease. Co-infection care must treat both viruses as one joint problem, not two separate ones.
plos-pone-0003554:
Magali Saint-Geniez and co-authors studied a growth factor's role in vision in this 2008 paper. VEGF is famous for building blood vessels, healthy and diseased alike. Evidence hinted it also acts directly on non-vascular cells. Anti-VEGF drugs are now widely used in eye care.

The team showed endogenous VEGF is required for visual function. It supports survival of Müller cells and of photoreceptors, the light sensors. Blocking VEGF too hard could starve the retina it should save. The finding urges care in dosing eye treatments. The same drugs also treat some cancers and lung diseases at higher stakes.
plos-pone-0003654:
M. Ángeles Serrano and Paolo De Los Rios published this network study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Flow networks move things along directed paths from input points to output points. Their large-scale shape decides how well the whole system works. The team asked what makes such networks efficient.

They studied percolated landscapes, where paths appear once enough links are in place. Their analysis links the layout of these networks to how much they can carry and how they change over time. The results apply to systems as unlike as water in rock and goods on roads.
plos-pone-0003754:
Ulrich Kirk published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. How much we like an object depends in part on the setting around it. Neuroimaging work had often studied context and perception, but less so beauty. Kirk used fMRI to watch aesthetic judgment at work.

He examined how the brain handles the link between an object and its context during judgment. The same image could please more or less depending on its frame. The study shows taste is not just in the object; the brain builds it from object and context together.
plos-pone-0003854:
Karim Hnia, Cécile Notarnicola, Pascal de Santa Barbara, and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Gastrokine-1 is a protein known from the stomach lining, and its role in smooth muscle cells was a mystery. To study it, the team first needed the native protein in pure form.

They established a protocol to purify gastrokine-1 from freshly dissected chicken gizzard smooth muscle. Then they characterized its biochemical properties, some of them unexpected. The groundwork sets up future study of what this protein actually does in muscle tissue.
plos-pone-0003954:
Joep P. M. Derikx, Dick A. van Waardenburg, Geertje Thuijls, and co-authors studied gut barrier loss during surgery in 2008. A leaking gut barrier is tied to complications after operations. Most study of that loss came from belly surgery itself. The team asked whether major surgery elsewhere also breaks the barrier.

Their PLOS ONE article followed twenty children having spinal fusion surgery. Spine surgery does not open the abdomen at all. Signs of gut barrier loss still developed in these patients. The finding widens concern about gut leakage to many major operations. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004054:
Elaine J. Gavin, Bo Song, Yuan Wang, and co-authors weakened a DNA protein in colon cancer cells in 2008. Their group had found Orc6 levels highly elevated in colon tumors. Orc6 also rose after treatment with the drug 5-fluorouracil. Those links made Orc6 a candidate drug target.

Their PLOS ONE article lowered Orc6 in human colon cancer cells. The cells then grew more sensitive to 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin. Pairing a target blocker with standard drugs could improve response. The work points to a combination strategy worth further testing. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004154:
Lane Yoder published this theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain's wiring is so vast and tangled that exact, fully specified networks have rarely been explored. As a result, how the pattern of synaptic connections shapes the way the brain handles information is poorly understood.

Building on a recently proposed model of the retina, Yoder designs explicit logic circuits, networks written out connection by connection. He tests whether such circuits can tell one neural state from another. The work offers a concrete way to link wiring diagrams to the computations a brain circuit performs.
plos-pone-0004254:
Makoto Honda and colleagues published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Narcolepsy is caused by the loss of most neurons that make hypocretin, also called orexin, the brain chemical that keeps us awake. The loss is believed to result from an autoimmune attack, but what actually kills the cells is unknown.

The team studied IGFBP3, a binding protein for growth factors, in relation to hypocretin. They report that IGFBP3 colocalizes with hypocretin and regulates it. A regulator sitting alongside the missing chemical gives researchers a new lead on the narcolepsy puzzle.
plos-pone-0004354:
Lina Rodahl and colleagues published this tumour genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Several regulators of endocytic trafficking, the system that sorts cargo inside cells, have lately been named tumour suppressors in Drosophila. These include components of the ESCRT machinery, which packages proteins for disposal. Breaking ESCRT subunits leads to enlarged cells and tissue overgrowth.

The team report that disrupting Vps4, an ESCRT partner, and JNK function in Drosophila causes tumour growth. Two systems that seem unrelated, waste sorting and stress signalling, collide in this route to cancer. The flies make the genetics fast and cheap to test.
plos-pone-0004454: In 2009, Ermakova, Shnol, and Panteleev modeled waves in flowing matter. Excitation waves in moving media were studied via the FitzHugh-Nagumo model. The flows bent the wave fronts sharply. The math serves blood-clotting and bioreactor models well. The work is purely theoretical.
plos-pone-0004554: In 2009, He, Wang, and Li built a clever protein-interaction text miner. PPI Finder mined human protein-protein interactions from the literature. The handy tool tamed the swelling publication flood. The method aids network biology research. The neat mining is text-based and fast.
plos-pone-0004654: In 2009, Pistis, Piras, and Pirastu found eight villages worlds apart by genes. Eight cut-off Sardinian villages showed big gene differences. The cut-off life molded distinct gene pools over time. The study helps future gene-link studies. The area is cut off still.
plos-pone-0004754: In 2009, Wiedemann, Loell, and Mueller found stomach-bug toxins sparking later trouble anew. H pylori cagpathogenicity islanddependent early immune response triggered later disease. The early immune response set the stage fully. The study maps gastric pathogenesis pathways. The needle system injects CagA.
florence-worcester-chronicle-forester-18:
Florence of Worcester kept his chronicle in the twelfth century, and Thomas Forester's 1854 English version carries it to modern readers. The tale runs from creation to 1141. Norman conquest and the anarchy of King Stephen's reign form its grim late chapters.

A monk who lived through civil war tells of kings, battles, and portents. Castles rise, towns burn, and chroniclers count the cost in famines. The work stands as a base source for medieval English history. Forester's version, in a popular series, made the chronicle a household book for Victorians who wanted their past in the words of those who saw it.
kircher-oedipus-aegyptiacus-vol3-1654:
Kircher sums up Egyptian wisdom in the third volume of Oedipus Aegyptiacus, in Latin from 1654. Real learning and fancied lore stand side by side in the vast close. The work forms the last great monument of Renaissance Hermeticism, splendid in dress and mistaken in many of its bold decipherments of the ancient signs.

No other book shows the old magical world view so fully arrayed. Kircher's Rome workshop drew reports from missions across the globe for it. Engravers, printers, and patrons all served his boundless design for years. Readers leave with awe at the scale of the attempt, if not belief in its answers.
noizet-memoire-somnambulisme-1854:
Francois-Joseph Noizet studies the magnetic sleep in his memoir on somnambulism, in French from 1854, though written back in 1820. The French general treats mesmerism with a soldier's order and a scholar's care. His early account ranks among the first scientific treatments of the strange sleep and its claimed wonders of sense.

He reports trials, failures, and puzzles without the showman's gloss. Publication waited decades while the subject ripened around his manuscript. Psychology might have grown faster had his road been taken sooner. The memoir stands as a road not taken in the field's history, sober proof that the magnetic sleep drew serious minds early.
treaty-of-kanagawa-1854:
Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy signed the Treaty of Kanagawa with Japan in March 1854. Perry had arrived with warships the year before, pressing Japan to end more than two centuries of near-total seclusion from the West. The talks took place under the shadow of those guns, and Japan's rulers knew refusal could mean war.

By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d154:
On 30 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, printed as Document 154 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter closed out a month of heavy mail between Washington and London.

September 1862 had brought Antietam and the emancipation plan, two events that reset foreign thinking about the war. British leaders put off any move to back the South, at least for the moment. Mail like this dispatch shows the steady pressure Washington kept on London while that choice hung in the balance through the autumn. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d254:
William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report on 21 February 1862, printed as Document 254 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris throughout this period.

Reports from Paris had a special flavor: Dayton dealt with a court where the emperor's wishes counted for more than public debate. He reported conversations, hints, and shifts of mood that rarely reached print in France. A February report like this one helped Washington judge whether Napoleon III meant to meddle in the war or only to watch it. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d354:
Edouard Thouvenel, the French foreign minister in Paris, wrote to Henri Mercier, his minister in Washington, on 19 January 1862. The instruction is printed as Document 354 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, among the French papers.

Thouvenel's letters were Mercier's orders, fixing the line France would take in Washington for weeks at a time. Seeing them in the American printed record lets readers watch French policy being made, not just received. This January instruction came as France settled into its solo course in Mexico and weighed the American war. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d454:
John Lothrop Motley in Vienna received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 September 1862. It is Document 454 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Seward wrote on the eve of Antietam, with Lee in Maryland and the fate of the autumn campaign undecided. Motley, in Vienna, had to hold the Union's line at a court that watched and waited. Instructions sent at such a moment stressed resolve above all. The dispatch belongs to the mid-September cluster in which Seward wrote to nearly every post in Europe. He was preparing his ministers for either result on the battlefield. He was also preparing them for the emancipation order he knew was coming.
frus-1862-d554:
On 6 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Belgium. The instruction is Document 554 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Sanford was among the most active of Seward's ministers, traveling, reporting, and watching Confederate agents wherever they surfaced in Europe. Orders to Brussels in May 1862 came as Union arms advanced and the government's case abroad improved. Belgium's own stake was trade and its king's wide influence. Seward used Sanford's energy gladly, feeding him the arguments and news the Brussels post needed. The dispatch is part of a correspondence marked by unusual warmth and frequency for so small a mission.
frus-1862-d654:
Dated 21 October 1861, this letter went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Townsend Harris, the American minister in Japan. It stands as document 654 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Harris would soon leave the post he had held since the legation opened.

Seward wrote to guide the men who spoke for the United States abroad. A letter like this one set out views from Washington that Harris was to use in his talks with Japan's rulers. Read with the rest of the file, it helps show how a small mission kept its footing while its home government fought for its life.
frus-1863p1-d54:
On 21 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to a Mr. Spence. Memminger was the Confederate secretary of the treasury in Richmond. The letter is document 54 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, among the Confederate papers printed in that volume.

The treasury's web reached into Britain, where agents and friends of the South worked on loans and sales of cotton. A letter like this one fed that web. It is dated the same week as Memminger's sheets to Mason in London, and it shares their theme: money, the South's scarcest weapon. Printed by the Union, it lets readers trace that hunt for cash in the foe's own words.
frus-1863p1-d154:
The pair of 13 April 1863 for London opens with this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 154 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-April pairs from Washington split the brief as it stood after the raider's seizure: hold the gain, watch the yards, mind the tone. Seward fed Adams those points sheet by sheet. This letter opens the pair of 13 April. It is desk work of a high order, brief in form and heavy in what it guarded.
frus-1863p1-d254:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 30 July 1863. It appears as document 254 of the 1863 papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d354:
Writing in Washington on 8 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 354 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d454:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 9 April 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d554:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 6 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d654:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 4 November 1863. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pone-0000154:
Elene R. Valdivia, Yajun Wu, Lian-Chao Li, and colleagues published this plant biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies a group-1 grass pollen allergen, a protein that also drives many hay fever cases. In maize, the authors test how this allergen affects pollen competition, the race between pollen grains to fertilize a flower.

A protein best known for making people sneeze turns out to matter in plant reproduction too. The authors measure its influence on which pollen wins. The work links an allergen's biology to plant breeding and to the spread of genes through maize populations, including questions about gene flow from crops.
plos-pone-0000254:
Per Unneberg and Jean-Michel Claverie published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tries a tentative mapping of interactions between chromosomes that are triggered by transcription, the reading of genes. Their data come from chimeric EST and mRNA sequences, messages that appear to join pieces from different chromosomes.

Chromosomes were once pictured as separate territories that rarely touch. Evidence of transcription-driven contact between them challenges that picture. The authors sift public sequence data for signs of such contact. The paper is exploratory, mapping a phenomenon that later work with new methods would test.
plos-pone-0000354:
Andy M. Reynolds and Mark A. Frye published this insect behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fruit flies track odors in free flight, zigzagging toward a food smell through moving air. The authors show this free-flight odor tracking is consistent with an optimal intermittent, scale-free search. Such a search is a pattern of bursts and pauses with no single characteristic scale.

A scale-free search is the best strategy when targets are sparse and clues are patchy. Showing flies match that optimum links their flight control to search theory. The result interests both biologists and engineers building small flying robots that must find odor sources.
plos-pone-0000454:
Yoshan Moodley and Michael W. Bruford argued for joining two fields to save Africa's wildlife, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Molecular biogeography uses DNA to map where species and their populations came from and how they are related across landscapes. The authors laid out a framework for conserving pan-African biodiversity built on that evidence.

Africa's wildlife crosses borders that conservation plans often respect more than animals do. DNA maps can show which populations are unique, which are connected, and where protection matters most. The paper is a call to integrate genetics into conservation decisions across the whole continent, rather than reserve by reserve.
plos-pone-0000554:
John Stephen Yap, Chenguang Wang, and Rongling Wu built a computational method described in PLOS ONE in 2007. It maps genes that shape how organisms handle heat. Thermal performance curves chart how well an organism grows or moves across temperatures. Their approach performs functional mapping of quantitative trait loci, the genome regions that regulate those curves.

A curve, not a single number, is the trait: genes may shift its peak, width, or height. Mapping such dynamic traits needs math that treats the whole curve at once. With climates warming, knowing which genes set thermal limits has direct ecological and agricultural stakes.
plos-pone-0000654:
Nathalie van der Velde, Bruno H. Ch. Stricker, Jos R. T. C. Roelandt and colleagues asked whether heart ultrasound can predict falls in older people. European and American guidelines call for echocardiography in patients with syncope, meaning fainting. Half of older adults with syncope present with a fall. Yet no published data had addressed heart scan findings in older fallers.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study set out to determine whether echocardiographic abnormalities mark those at risk. Falls injure and kill many older adults, so any test that flags risk early has value. The study tests whether a scan already used for fainting can do double duty for fall prevention.
plos-pone-0000754:
Renata Freitas, GuangJun Zhang and Martin J. Cohn found an old pattern of gene activity in shark fins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The evolution of limbs from fins required new distal structures, the digits at the far end. In four-limbed animals, genes at one end of the HoxD cluster switch on in two distinct phases during limb development. The second phase builds the digit region.

Shark paired fins, the authors show, also display this biphasic Hoxd expression. That pushes the distal limb domain's origin far back, before fins became limbs. Sharks are not primitive leftovers here; their development preserves the ancient program that digits later inherited.
plos-pone-0000854:
Stephanie D. Shaw, Sutapa Chakrabarti, Gourisankar Ghosh and colleagues trimmed a splicing factor and found it still worked, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Serine/arginine-rich proteins, called SR proteins, are essential splicing factors. They carry one or two RNA-recognition motifs and a tail rich in arginine and serine, the RS domain. SR proteins bind splicing enhancers in the RNA and were thought to promote splicing from that position, using the RS domain.

Deleting the N-terminus of the SR protein SF2/ASF permitted splicing independent of the RS domain, their title reports. A part thought indispensable turns out dispensable after trimming. Results like this revise the mechanics textbooks give for splicing.
plos-pone-0000954:
Dietmar Dirnberger and Klaus Seuwen tested whether human frizzled receptors can talk to a yeast mating pathway, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Frizzled receptors span the cell membrane seven times, like the large GPCR family, but they are classed as atypical members. Yeast mating runs through a classic GPCR system, making yeast a handy test bed.

By placing human frizzled receptors into that system, the pair could watch for signaling in a clean setting. Yeast offers a blank background, free of the many partners found in human cells. Results from such swaps help sort which receptors truly couple to G proteins, a question with direct drug relevance.
plos-pone-0001054:
David Plachetzki, Bernard Degnan and Todd Oakley traced how new protein partnerships arose in animal eyes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Biologists increasingly understand the genetic bases of change in form. The origins of traits built on brand new protein interactions, though, remain largely undocumented.

Opsins are the light catching proteins of vision, and their partners decide what an eye can do with light. The team analyze opsin evolution across animals to catch new interactions as they arose. A documented origin is worth more than a plausible story. Their case gives eye evolution a rare before and after record.
plos-pone-0001154:
DNA barcoding uses a short stretch of DNA to identify a species, much as a barcode identifies a product. Chodon Sass and colleagues tested whether proposed barcodes work for cycads, an ancient group of plants, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Barcodes are most needed when a specimen lacks the features used for visual identification.

The authors evaluated the candidate marker sequences for telling cycad species apart. Reliable barcodes could become a forensic tool for conservation, since many cycads are endangered and traded illegally. Their tests show how well the proposed markers perform in this plant group.
plos-pone-0001254:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is the most common motor neuron disease, currently incurable, with treatment largely limited to supportive care. Katrina Gwinn and colleagues survey the genetics of the disease in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They also call for a new era of collaborative gene discovery. Family history raises the risk of ALS, and many inherited causes had already been found.

The authors argue that progress now depends on groups pooling samples and data, since each individual cause is rare. Their piece is a perspective on how ALS research should organize itself. It reflects a shift toward large consortia in human genetics.
plos-pone-0001354:
In mature neurons, the genes for MHC class I are repressed. These genes encode the immune system's identity-display molecules. Neurons are normally invisible to immune patrols in this respect. Julie Miralvès and colleagues studied a repressor behind that silence, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. MeCP2 is a protein that binds methylated DNA and represses genes; its own gene's mutations cause Rett syndrome.

The authors report that high levels of MeCP2 depress MHC class I expression in neuronal cells. The MHC genes are rich in the CpG sites MeCP2 reads. Their finding links a famous neurodevelopmental protein to immune invisibility in the brain.
plos-pone-0001454:
Tadashi Nomura and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on what makes the mammal cortex unique. The cortex has six neat layers of nerve cells, built in a set order as the embryo grows. No other class of backboned animal has a true match for it. The team asked which growth traits make this layered build possible.

They point to the pattern of nerve cell birth and to the level of a guide protein called Reelin. Both traits prove vital for a mammal type cortex to form. The work helps explain how a new brain design arose in evolution. It also frames why faults in these steps cause grave brain ills.
plos-pone-0001554:
Hoau-Yan Wang, Maya Frankfurt, and Lindsay Burns published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on opioid tolerance. Very low doses of opioid blockers can boost pain relief and cut tolerance. They do so by stopping a switch in how the opioid receptor links to its cell partners. Where the blocker binds to force that was not known.

The team show the blocker binds a protein called filamin A with high strength. That bind is the grip that stops the switch. A named grip gives drug teams a clear target. Drugs built on it could hold pain relief longer with less dose gain and less dependence.
plos-pone-0001654:
Marta Pires de Miranda and co-authors dissected a virus protein that hijacks B-cell signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gammaherpesviruses set up lifelong latent infections in B cells, the antibody-making cells of the immune system. To do so, they switch on pathways that normally sit below the B-cell receptor. One such viral tool is m2, a protein of murine gammaherpesvirus 68.

The team shows that m2 gathers several cell proteins at once, a multi-docking assembly. It bends the Fyn and Vav signaling pathway to the virus's ends. The full text gives the binding tests and the signals they recorded. Knowing how a virus imitates the cell's own switches helps explain how these infections persist for life. The question also bears on the human gammaherpesviruses.
plos-pone-0001754:
Emma L. Meczes, Kathryn L. Gilroy, Katherine L. West, and their co-authors studied a tail piece of a DNA-handling enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Type II DNA topoisomerases are essential enzymes that solve tangles arising as DNA is copied and read. They pass one double helix through a temporary break in another, powered by ATP.

The team measured the impact of the human enzyme's C-terminal domain, its tail region, on activity. The full text gives the enzyme assays with and without the tail and what changed. These enzymes are targets of major cancer drugs, so knowing which parts control activity can help design drugs and explain resistance.
plos-pone-0001854:
Lieven Thorrez, Katrijn Van Deun, Léon-Charles Tranchevent, and their co-authors warned against a common lab shortcut in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Housekeeping genes are needed in every tissue, since their expression is required for cell survival, integrity, or duplication. They are commonly used as reference genes to normalize gene expression data, on the assumption that they are expressed at constant levels.

Using ribosomal protein genes as the test case, the team shows that assumption can fail: reference genes vary more than users expect. The full text gives the expression data across tissues. Bad normalization quietly distorts thousands of published gene measurements, so this cautionary tale has unusual reach.
plos-pone-0001954:
Francois van Loggerenberg and co-authors described the work of building a high-risk HIV study group in South Africa, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The group, part of the CAPRISA 002 study of acute infection, follows people at high risk so that new infections can be caught early. Such groups are the base for vaccine and prevention trials.

Between August 2004 and May 2005, the team enrolled the cohort and recorded its health and social profile. They also report new infection rates and the hard parts of keeping such a group intact. Honest accounts of these hurdles help later trials plan for real life.
plos-pone-0002054:
Sanjeev Mahanta and co-authors found the smallest piece of a cancer-linked protein that drives growth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, MUC1, is made in abnormal form on many solid tumors. On healthy lining cells it clusters at the top face only; on cancer cells it spreads over the whole surface. A direct link from that change to cancer growth had been elusive.

The team whittled MUC1 down to a minimal fragment. As the title states, that fragment alone mediates the growth of cancer cells. A small active piece is a cleaner drug target than a huge protein.
plos-pone-0002154:
Melissa Bowlin and Martin Wikelski measured the true flight costs of migrating songbirds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Migrant birds, bats, and insects tend to have more pointed wings than species that stay put. Pointed wings and low wing loading were thought to save energy on long flights. Low wing loading means low body mass per wing area. The idea had never been tested directly.

Bowlin and Wikelski report that pointed wings, low wing loading, and calm air each cut the cost of migratory flight. Their tests turn a long-held guess about wing shape into measured fact. The results help explain why long-distance migrants look the way they do.
plos-pone-0002254:
Lina Guerra and co-authors used a bacterial toxin to find a key player in the response to DNA damage, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When adherent cells meet DNA-damaging agents, such as the bacterial cytolethal distending toxin or radiation, they switch on the small protein RhoA. RhoA builds stress fibers and delays cell death, but the signals between damage and RhoA were missing.

The team identifies Net1, a factor that activates RhoA, as a key effector in that response. Filling in the chain from DNA damage to cell survival helps explain how cells buy time to repair themselves. How cancer cells may abuse the same delay.
plos-pone-0002354:
Ziyin Li and co-authors found a new passenger complex that guides cell division in a parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Aurora B kinase is a key part of the chromosomal passenger complex, which steers chromosome segregation and the final split of one cell into two. In Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind sleeping sickness, an Aurora B relative was known but its partners were missing.

The team identifies a novel chromosomal passenger complex in the parasite. They also show it takes a unique position during cytokinesis, the final split. A division machine that differs from the human one is attractive for drugs that must kill the parasite, not the patient.
plos-pone-0002454:
In 2008, Desmond and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Chris Desmond, Ruth M. Bland, Gerard Boyce, and others. Its subject is scaling-Up Exclusive Breastfeeding Support Programmes: The Example of KwaZulu-Natal. Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for six months is the mainstay of global child health.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002554:
A research team led by Stoel reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Berend C. Stoel, Terry M. Borman, and others. Its subject is a Comparison of Wood Density between Classical Cremonese and Modern Violins. Classical violins created by Cremonese masters, such as Antonio Stradivari and Giuseppe Guarneri Del Gesu.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002654:
Jayabalan M. Joseph led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the actinome of dictyostelium discoideum in comparison to actins and Actin-Related proteins from other organisms. Authorship is credited in the record to Jayabalan M. Joseph and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Actin belongs to the most abundant proteins in eukaryotic cells which harbor usually many conventional actin isoforms as well as actin-related proteins (Arps). Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002754:
Chiara Pastori led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was arterially perfused Neurosphere-Derived cells distribute outside the ischemic core in a model of transient focal ischemia and reperfusion in vitro. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Chiara Pastori, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Treatment with neural stem cells represents a potential strategy to improve functional recovery of post-ischemic cerebral injury. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002854:
Thomas A. Terleph led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was response properties of the auditory telencephalon in songbirds change with recent experience and season. The catalog record names Thomas A. Terleph first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) is a telencephalic auditory area that is selectively activated by conspecific vocalizations in zebra finches and canaries. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002954:
Paul Makidon, Anna Bielinska, Shraddha Nigavekar and co-authors tested a new hepatitis B vaccine form in animals in 2008. Hepatitis B stays a major global health problem despite safe, effective vaccines. Current vaccines need cold storage and three shots, which restricts use where clinics are scarce.

Their candidate uses a nanoemulsion, a mix of tiny oil droplets, given through the nose as a mucosal vaccine. Pre-clinical evaluation means testing before human trials. Published in PLOS ONE, the work explores a form that could ease delivery in the developing world if later trials support it.
plos-pone-0003054:
Paul Medina, Ryan Worthen, Lawrence Forsberg and co-authors studied dendrite upkeep in neurons in 2008. Neurons need precise control of their inner skeleton: microtubule tracks carry cargo in axons and dendrites, while actin organizes synapses. Their unique shape makes neurons especially sensitive to faults in that system.

The actin-binding protein Capulet genetically interacts with the microtubule motor kinesin to maintain dendrite homeostasis, the title reports. Pairing an actin factor with a microtubule motor shows the two systems cooperate. Published in PLOS ONE, dendrite stability underpins learning circuits and their disorders. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003154:
Georgiy Bobashev, Robert J. Morris and D. Michael Goedecke examine airport networks in epidemic models in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Models of global spread for flu, SARS and tuberculosis often treat a sample of international airports as the network that carries disease. Yet there was no agreement on how that sample should be chosen.

The authors study sampling choices and the topology, or shape, of an international airport network. Readers see why the airports picked can change what a model predicts. The work matters for planners who rely on such models to judge how fast a new infection might travel around the world.
plos-pone-0003254:
Natasha Webb, Geoff Connolly, Judy Tellam and colleagues reassess a virus pathway claim in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Previous studies had indicated that Epstein-Barr virus can modulate the Wnt pathway in virus-infected cells, and that this effect is mediated by the viral oncogene latent membrane protein 1, or LMP1. The team reassessed the role of LMP1 in regulating expression of various pathway components.

The title reports that Epstein-Barr virus modulation of the Wnt pathway is not dependent on LMP1. Readers see a causal credit reassigned after a direct check. Such corrections keep virus cancer research from building on the wrong viral protein.
plos-pone-0003354:
Ingrid Masse, Laurent Molin, Laurent Mouchiroud and colleagues find a new lifespan factor in worms in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The PTEN tumour suppressor encodes a phosphatase, and its daf-18 orthologue in Caenorhabditis elegans negatively regulates the insulin and IGF-1 DAF-2 receptor pathway that influences lifespan in worms and other species. The team set out to identify new DAF-18 regulated pathways involved in lifespan.

The title reports a novel role for the SMG-1 kinase in lifespan and oxidative stress resistance in C. elegans. Readers get another gene in the ageing network beyond insulin signaling alone. Worm lifespan genes often nominate pathways later found in mammals.
plos-pone-0007454: Mass spectrometry now lets biologists measure thousands of proteins at once, but the math for analyzing the data has lagged behind. This study builds a statistical framework using empirical Bayes methods — a way to borrow strength across measurements — for protein-counting experiments. Better analysis tools mean the flood of protein data can finally be turned into reliable biology.
plos-pone-0007554: The isolated valley of Val Borbera in Italy offers geneticists a gift: a large population with shared environment and simpler genetics. This study mapped heritability and family structure there, showing why such isolates make hunting complex-trait genes easier. The valley becomes a natural laboratory for finding genes behind common diseases.
plos-pone-0007654: DNA's packaging into chromatin follows a code written into the sequence itself. This study catalogued the two-letter DNA combinations that position nucleosomes — the spools DNA wraps around. The inventory refines our reading of the chromatin code layered atop the genetic one.
plos-pone-0007754: Nerve fibers work best with a precise ratio of insulation to core — the g-ratio. This theoretical study calculated the optimal value for the rat central nervous system. The number gives biologists a benchmark for healthy myelination.
plos-pone-0007854: A blood meal floods a mosquito with iron and toxins, yet its flight muscles keep working. This study found blood-feeding triggers reversible changes in the mitochondria of Aedes aegypti flight muscle. The temporary rewiring shows how the mosquito survives its own dinner.
plos-pone-0007954: Retreating tuberculosis often fails where drug resistance runs high. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Matthys and colleagues tracked outcomes of the WHO Category II retreatment regimen in a population rife with drug-resistant TB. Standard short-course therapy falters against resistant strains. The outcome data question whether the standard retreatment recipe still works in such settings.
plos-pone-0008054: Mouse geneticists received a cleaner cutting tool. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Wu and colleagues engineered mice carrying an improved FLPo gene-snipping enzyme on the widely used C57BL/6J background. Tools like FLP let researchers delete or swap genes in specific tissues at chosen times, but older versions worked sluggishly. The upgraded FLPo cuts DNA more reliably, giving scientists finer control. The new mouse line should speed up the routine genetic manipulations behind much of modern biomedical research.
plos-pone-0008154: A childhood cancer's master regulator was mapped genome-wide. This 2009 study analyzed MYCN transcription factor binding in neuroblastoma, finding association with distinct DNA motifs and hypermethylated regions. The map exposes how this oncogene hijacks the genome.
plos-pone-0008254: Hepatitis C got a broad-antibody hope. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Mancini's team found human antibodies that hit all HCV genotypes. Conserved viral spots are rare prizes. The broad hits were mapped. The hope feeds vaccine design.
plos-pone-0008354: Gene switches got split into two keys. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hirrlinger's team built split-CreERT2, a Cre system in two halves that only works when rejoined.
